body: Tetlock, 'Expert Political Judgment' (2005): about 28,000 predictions by 284 experts over two decades. Experts barely beat simple extrapolation and were often worse than chance on long horizons. 'Foxes' (eclectic, self-critical, probabilistic) beat 'hedgehogs' (one big theory), and the most famous hedgehogs were the worst calibrated. Mellers et al., 'Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament' (Psychological Science 25(5), 2014; ~280 S2 citations): in the IARPA tournament (thousands of forecasters, hundreds of questions, 2011-2013), the Good Judgment Project beat the competing teams by a wide margin. Three interventions improved Brier-score accuracy: an hour of training in probabilistic reasoning (use base rates, avoid biases), about 10% better; working in teams that share reasoning; and 'tracking', placing the top 2% ('superforecasters') together, who improved further and stayed top year after year. Skill persisted, so it was not luck. Superforecaster habits: start from the base rate (outside view), then adjust; update often in small steps; use fine-grained probabilities (60% vs 65% mattered; Friedman et al. 2018); keep score. Replicated: the tournament results are robust across years; later work (Karvetski et al.) shows forecast rationales predict accuracy. Use for us: write every thesis as dated, explicit probabilities ('P(revenue CAGR >20% FY26-29) = 35%'), score them with Brier scores in the decision log, and review calibration yearly. Foxes over hedgehogs: avoid one-theme convictions (for example 'defence will re-rate forever').

data.method: base rate -> adjust -> frequent small updates -> score

title: Superforecasting (Tetlock; Mellers et al. 2014): training, teaming and tracking beat experts; foxes beat hedgehogs; calibration can be learned
